items.title: For Centuries, Cave Visitors Walked Right by 280 Ice Age Engravings. The Newly Discovered Rock Art Is Rewriting Catalonia's Prehistory
items.desc: Prior to the discovery, rock art in northeastern Spain was "very scarce," one archaeologist says. The drawings show dozens of animals, as well as more abstract shapes, which are distinct from other Paleolithic styles
items.text:
Christian Thorsberg | Daily Correspondent
Tourists, explorers, archaeologists and others have been visiting the Cova de la Font Major , a cave system in Catalonia, Spain, since at least the 12th century. They’ve explored two miles of underground caves and rivers; left graffiti; and even opened a museum in the 1990s.
But it wasn’t until recently that a team of archaeologists discovered what, for centuries, these relatively modern visitors had apparently failed to notice. Hidden in plain sight, left behind by some of the cave’s very first inhabitants, was the third-largest collection of Ice Age-era engravings to have ever been found on the Mediterranean side of the Iberian Peninsula.
“At the moment of discovery, I experienced a mixture of excitement at encountering something both unexpected and extraordinary and profound disbelief,” Josep Maria Vergès , an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES), tells Gizmodo ’s Gayoung Lee. “It seemed inconceivable that none of the many visitors who had traversed the gallery … had ever noticed the presence of these prehistoric engravings.”
During a series of excavations in 2019, researchers from IPHES identified some 280 Paleolithic engravings on the cave’s walls. The motifs were wide-ranging, comprising 55 distinct animals—horses, a bear, deer and early types of wild cattle among them—and dozens of abstract patterns, lines and loops. Their research was published this week in the journal Antiquity .
A post shared by Antiquity Journal (@antiquityjournal)
Paleolithic rock art on the Iberian peninsula is plentiful but unevenly distributed. Prior to the discovery at Cova de la Font Major, rock art identified in Catalonia was “very scarce compared with the abundant record of the neighboring Franco-Cantabrian region,” Vergès explains in a statement .
It remains unclear how the markings had never been documented before. They are in a part of the cave that has been open to tourists since 1957. The general consensus was that the walls of the cave were too “irregular both in relief and color” to preserve art, per the article.
The researchers speculate that lighting may have had a role to play in the belated discovery. “When you shine a light straight on the engravings, they are really difficult to see. You have to play with light from different directions to see the depressions,” Míriam Salas-Altès , an archaeologist with IPHES and a co-author of the study, tells Nature ’s Chris Simm

Listening to The Womack Sisters feels like you’ve put on a record from the 1960s, a time when pop and soul engaged in a juicy, alluring collaboration. Despite their seemingly vintage sound, they are actually contemporary group made up of sisters Kucha, Zeimani, and BG Womack. With their rich voices and a knack for producing ear worms, they have created a collection of effortlessly timeless tracks that speak to modern sensibilities, tending a musical bridge between past and present.
Many would say it’s in their blood, as the sisters come from music royalty. Their parents are Cecil and Linda Womack, who made up the influential duo Womack & Womack. As such, the three of them grew up on the road, performing with their family on stages all over the world from a young age. Their uncle, Bobby Womack, was also prolific R&B songwriter and their maternal grandfather was Sam Cooke, long considered The King of Soul.
Though they had a keen understanding of music business, deciphering how to break into the industry was still an uphill battle. After years of jumping between London, Thailand, Paris, Amsterdam, and Johannesburg, the Womack sisters arrived in LA determined to kickstart their music career. To do this, they had to balance day jobs with their craft. Even so, the sisters looked at the bright side, finding inspiration in their time as Uber drivers to make ends meet for their hit “ Chauffeur .”
After years of hard work and resisting the industry’s idea that soul music wouldn’t get them far, The Womack Sisters recently released their debut album under Daptone Records. The record has received positive reviews, commending its tight songwriting, punchy arrangements, and overall cheerful sentiment, even when the sisters touch on more difficult topics. Critics have also noted how the sisters are clearly inspired by their family’s legacy but are never constrained by it; instead, they are uplifted by it to find their own voice. Their sound also carries the spirit of Amy Winehouse, who they are big fans of.
You can check out their self-titled debut album on Spotify . Their U.S. tour kicks off next month and wraps up in January 2027. In a major achievement, they will also be opening for Harry Styles at his Chicago residency next year.
To stay up to date with them, follow The Womack Sisters on Instagram .

items.title: 75 People Who Got Married And Then Learned Something They Definitely Wish They Knew Earlier
items.desc: Getting married is a serious commitment. That’s why couples usually spend plenty of time getting to know each other and figuring out whether they’re truly compatible before tying the knot. But no matter how long you’ve been together, there’s no guarantee you’ve learned absolutely everything about your partner. Redditors shared the things they only discovered about their spouses after getting marri
items.text:
How long should two people be together before deciding to get married? Some couples are ready to say “I do” after just a few months, while others spend years dating before taking the next step.
Of course, there’s no universal timeline that works for everyone. Still, it’s interesting to see just how much the average length of a relationship before marriage can vary depending on where you live.
For example, according to The Knot , American couples who married in 2025 had dated for an average of three years before getting engaged . Meanwhile, a 2024 survey by British wedding planning platform Bridebook found that couples in the UK spent an average of 4.7 years together before getting engaged.
And that’s without counting the engagement itself, which can add another year or two before the wedding finally takes place.
But marriage traditions look quite different in other parts of the globe. In India, for instance, arranged marriages remain common, meaning couples may have considerably less time to get acquainted beforehand.
According to data from the India Human Development Survey of 2011–2012, nearly 65% of surveyed married women had met their husbands only at or around the time of marriage. Just 11% reported having known their husbands for more than a year or since childhood.
So, does spending more time together before marriage actually increase your chances of staying happily married? There is some research suggesting that it might.
A study by economists at Emory University, involving more than 3,000 people who had been married, found that those who dated for at least three years before getting engaged were less likely to divorce than those who dated for less than a year.
However, this doesn’t necessarily mean that dating longer prevents divorce, as other factors could also explain why these couples were more likely to stay married.
Interestingly, there’s also evidence that couples who spend very little time together before marriage can be just as happy.
A 2012 study published in Psychological Reports compared 28 people in arranged marriages with 30 in love-based marriages among Indian adults living in the United States. Researchers found no significant differences in their reported levels of marital satisfaction, love, or commitment.
Of course, the study was relatively small, but its findings suggest that the way a couple gets together doesn’t necessarily determine how happy they’ll be.

items.text:
Photo: © teamLab Architects, Vincent Hecht
The international art collective teamLab is celebrating the first anniversary of teamLab Biovortex Kyoto , its largest museum in Japan. Since opening on October 7, 2025, the immersive art destination has welcomed more than 1.3 million visitors from 167 countries and regions, highlighting the international draw of interactive art that blends technology, creativity, and participation.
The museum’s reach extends well beyond Japan. International visitors account for approximately 44% of total attendance, with many traveling from the United States, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Germany. Guests also spend more than two and a half hours exploring its spaces on average, reflecting how deeply they engage with the experience.
Guided by the concept Universe of Existence, Universe of Perception , the museum examines how people experience their surroundings through interactive digital environments. Rather than simply viewing artworks, visitors become active participants. In Athletics Forest , movement shapes an immersive, multidimensional space, while Future Park invites guests to collaborate through hands-on artmaking. Both projects reflect teamLab’s educational focus on learning through participation.
To mark the anniversary, the museum is presenting Vanishing Tree and Wildflowers , featuring Japanese fantail willow. The temporary installation runs from October 7 through October 11, 2026, adding a special presentation to the milestone celebration.
Kyoto Mayor Koji Matsui has also recognized the museum’s contribution to the city’s cultural landscape, including its role in promoting the arts and supporting the southeastern area around Kyoto Station. The museum’s international attendance underscores how contemporary art can bring global audiences into conversation with Kyoto’s cultural identity.

Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide is celebrated among the creative community for her enigmatic yet eye-catching visual language. Her unique blend of mysticism, tradition, and identity, mostly shot in black and white, has earned Iturbide a place among the upper echelons of contemporary photography. Now, in recognition of her life’s work, Iturbide has been inducted into the Leica Hall of Fame.
The photographic equipment company has commended Iturbide’s oeuvre as, “Iconic images that have become etched into the collective memory are a testament to their work, touching the viewer and illustrating the ‘conditio humana’ in a timeless manner.” Iturbide is the first Latin American photographer to receive this honor, joining other legendary creatives like Steve McCurry, Joel Meyerowitz, Walter Vogel, Barbara Klemm, and Nick Út.
Born in Mexico City in 1942, Iturbide was immersed in photography from a young age, as her father was a devoted amateur photographer. She also surrounded herself with some of the most innovative creatives in her home country, working as an assistant to photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo for a year. The death of her six-year-old daughter Claudia had a profound effect on her, prompting her to pursue a career as a professional photographer. In 1975, at age 33, she celebrated her first photographic exhibit in her hometown, and opened her first New York show the following year.
For the photographer, a picture’s quality has less to do with composition and more with what it can awaken in the viewer. “Difficult to say what a good photograph is made of. But for me, a good picture is the one that makes the other person feel something,” Iturbide says. items.text:
A man who received nothing but hate mail for his Halloween hobby proved to be just the treat that Tammy Wyche needed to brighten her weekly drive to cancer treatment appointments.
Though a front yard covered in skeletons might serve to remind someone of their mortality, Wyche marveled at the creativity with which the homeowner arranged his decorations.
Some were raising the flag at Iwo Jima, while another was giving its dog a bone. There was a bony beekeeper who stood behind a cowboy riding an osseous equine, not far from where two boneheaded tourists were taking a selfie.
Yet despite this macabre menagerie, the scariest thing to Mr. Bill Pyle was what tended to show up in his Oxford, Ohio mailbox in those weeks leading up to Halloween—accusations of devil worship, promises of his expedient arrival in hell, and other such condemnations.
This carried on year after year, until one fateful day when Pyle opened a letter that he said stopped him “dead in his tracks.”
“I have been driving past your house daily for the past 19 days on my way to radiation treatments. A highlight of my journey has been checking to see who else has joined the bone family & what they are up to,” Wyche wrote in a heartfelt, handwritten correspondence.
“Thankfully, Wed. Sept 11th is my final radiation treatment, though I may need to continue to drive by once in a while to see what’s new. Thanks for the diversion.”
“Tears came to my eyes,” Pyle told CBS News’ ‘On the Road’ with Steve Hartman, remembering when he read it the first time. “[It]really touched my heart.”
Seeing the date of her final treatment, Pyle decided to roll the bones on a big surprise for this special admirer.
When Wyche drove past the ‘Bone Family’ that Wednesday morning, she looked to the right and saw a whole skeleton crew cheering her on with signs that celebrated this final milestone.
“It was very touching to think that somebody would go to that effort for a stranger,” she said.
Thanks to the story of Wyche’s brush with death at Pyle’s house, for every one person that has a bone to pick with him, there are 30—from as far away as Australia—sending messages of appreciation that encourage him to keep going with his skeletons.

items.title: Print commissioned by Nasa uncovered for exhibition
items.desc: The Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition tells the story of the British International Print Biennale.
items.text:
Komtek I (left) was created in 1968 from an early computer image
A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.
Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.
The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.
The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.
While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.
"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.
"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.
In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.
John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.
Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.
He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.
Cartwright Hall is home to one of Andy Warhol's famous Marilyn prints
Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.
It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.
Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.
Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.

items.desc: Brands including Dr Martens, Nike and Coach are among those using recycled materials.
items.text:
Gen Phoenix in Peterborough transforms leather offcuts into a new lower-carbon fabric, used by brands such as Dr Martens and Coach
How many clothes, items of bedding and other fabric have you thrown away this year?
While resale sites are growing in popularity, in the UK we still bin about 711,000 tonnes of textiles annually , external – roughly the weight of seven US aircraft carriers , external .
The global fashion and textiles industry is one of the most wasteful, but recycling firms in Peterborough and Northamptonshire are using technology to change that.
They are gaining the attention of major brands but say they need laws, as well as consumers, to support them.
New EU legislation requires fashion brands on sale there to demonstrate the sustainability of their products
In a warehouse next to the A14 in Kettering, a mountain of crumpled fabric is slowly fed into a machine.
There are dressing gowns, duvets, branded banners and lanyards from events including the Commonwealth Games.
All are made from polyester – the world's most commonly used textile fibre – and all have been thrown away.
Traditionally they would be burned or buried in landfill but Project Re:Claim is trying to change that.
The partnership between The Salvation Army's trading arm (SATCoL) and Plan B Circular operates what they say is the first commercial-scale polyester textile-to-textile recycling facility in Europe – technology adapted from a bottle recycling plant.

The Salvation Army collects the items and those that cannot be reused in their current form are shredded and melted.

"It's the future: using the clothing we have today to make the clothing that we need tomorrow," says Plan B Circular founder Tim Cross.
"We process 500kg of fabric an hour but we could easily scale up if there was demand.

In a war driven by drones and battlefield sensors, access to space is essential. After Starlink speed restrictions and Russian Oreshnik missile strikes, Kyiv is racing to develop its own space capabilities
For people in the Russian industrial city of Samara on the banks of the Volga, the first they knew of the Ukrainian attack were detonations that sent a column of smoke into the air.
If the Kremlin was vague about the target, video footage on social media soon made it clear what had been hit in the early hours of 15 August: the Progress Rocket and Space Centre, manufacturer of Russia’s Soyuz-2 rockets.
Two Flamingo missiles had slammed into a pair of buildings, including a facility known as 106A, a “clean room” where motherboards for the Soyuz launch systems were assembled.
In the midst of other Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries and industry, the Samara attack stood out, providing evidence of a spreading war, the geographical impact of which – already felt across Europe via hybrid attacks, and assaults on civilian shipping in the Black Sea – has crept into the domain of space.
In a conflict that is redefining warfare through the heavy use of drones and battlefield sensors, access to space and the satellites that power those systems – as well as the ability to disrupt enemy operations there – has become ever more critical.
The attack on Samara was a case in point, hitting the rockets that deliver Russia’s new Rassvet satellite system, which is being rapidly deployed as a replacement for Elon Musk’s Starlink, from which Russia was shut out earlier this year.
In addition, Ukraine has attacked other sites belonging to Roscosmos this year, including Korolyov, a large complex north of Moscow, and a Ukrainian-built radio telescope captured by Russia in Crimea.
Russia’s attempts to rapidly deploy its Rassvet network are not the only challenge from space that Ukraine faces. Moscow has also used Oreshnik ballistic missiles on at least three occasions – a system that launches into near space, then deploys multiple independently targetable warheads initially designed for nuclear weapons.
All of this has prompted Kyiv to intensify efforts to diversify its own access to space-based systems away from the US and Starlink, which was controversially choked in recent weeks, and to develop new space countermeasures against threats such as the Oreshnik.

items.title: This Wooden Wardrobe in Pompeii Remained Sealed for Nearly 2,000 Years. Archaeologists Just Opened It for the First Time
items.desc: The ancient cabinet held a pair of tweezers, a perfume bottle, an incense burner and ceramic vessels. But the most impressive find was a necklace sporting at least 24 amulets shaped like deities, plants and body parts
items.text:
Meilan Solly | Senior Associate Digital Editor, History
Nearly 2,000 years ago, residents of the ancient Roman city of Pompeii stashed an eclectic mix of objects in a wooden wardrobe. The trove boasted both utilitarian items, such as a bronze lamp, and personal treasures, including a necklace featuring at least two dozen miniature charms and a cache of 38 coins. Now, archaeologists have unearthed these artifacts in a house on one of Pompeii’s busiest streets .
Based on the number of valuables found in the wardrobe, archaeologists suspect that the house’s owners left in a hurry, perhaps during the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. (Most of the bronze coins date to the time of the Roman emperor Nero , who reigned between 54 and 68, and the frescoes adorning the building’s rooms correspond with the fourth style of Roman wall painting , which was popular between 20 and 79.) Whatever the reason for these Pompeians’ departure, they never returned home to retrieve their belongings.
“We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of whoever lived ⁠in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily life,” says Gabriel Zuchtriegel , director of the Archaeological Park of Pompeii, in a statement , per a translation by Reuters ’ Crispian Balmer. “The ​value of this discovery lies in the possibility of reading together the different traces ​of a ⁠life: personal habits, work and memories.”
Archaeologists uncovered the wardrobe while surveying the House of Cornelius Maximus , a building in central Pompeii that was first excavated in 1912. As Zuchtriegel and his colleagues write in the archaeological park’s online journal , the cabinet’s contents paint a portrait of domestic life in the doomed city, revealing the range of activities that took place in ancient Roman homes.
Several artifacts recovered from the site are characteristic of mundus muliebris , a Latin term that refers to “objects intended for the personal care and adornment of women in the Roman world,” in the words of historian Pilar Pavón . These items include a pair of tweezers, a mortar used to prepare makeup pigments, and a glass balsamarium that once held perfume or scented oils.
In addition to these beauty accessories, archaeologists found bronze, glass and ceramic vessels that were likely used for cooking and dining. A post shared by Сабир Ахмедов (@sabir_park)
Birds share our everyday spaces, but we rarely take the time to really notice how they’ve adapted to living among us. NIDIUM by SPLACES.STUDIO is an ongoing series of nest-like, audio-reactive sculptures that invite us to pause and listen to birdsong .
The name NIDIUM comes from the Latin word for “nest.” The installation series comprises 20 unique public sculptures of varying sizes, measuring between 2.5 and 4 meters (8.2 to 13.1 feet) in diameter. Woven from cultivated willow, each larger-than-life nest is interlaced with warm strips of LED lighting and emits a continuous soundscape of birdsong recorded in Karelia, between northwestern Russia and Finland.
Each sculpture “listens” to the sounds around it, responding with its own unique soundscape based on human voices and movements. This creates a playful two-way conversation between people and nature, helping observers become more aware of the wildlife sharing their surroundings.
The series is a collaborative effort, brought to life by artist Andre Svibovitch , light engineer Nikita Boyak , floral artist Sabir Ahmedov , sound programmer Vsevolod Krassa, and neural network specialist Igor Prudnikov. Each sculpture is individually programmed and made with slightly different forms, allowing the giant nests to fit into a range of locations, from urban environments to exhibition spaces. So far, NIDIUM installations have appeared in skyscrapers and public spaces across St. Petersburg, as well as at Bolzano Art Week and various exhibitions throughout Europe and North America.

items.text:
Applications due on 3 December for new generation of explorers who can ‘shape humanity’s future in space’
Nasa has launched a callout for a new generation of astronauts as it searches for explorers who could live and work on the moon.
Opening applications for the latest expansion of its Artemis program , the US agency said successful candidates would help “shape humanity’s future in space” as it builds a base on the moon and plans the first crewed missions to Mars.
The news was announced on Saturday during a Kennedy Space Center air show promoting lunar exploration, as well as advances in aviation and technology.
“This is an extraordinary time to join Nasa’s astronaut corps,” said Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman. “The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars.”
Nasa expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training the next class of astronaut candidates. The agency last opened applications for new astronauts in 2024, ultimately accepting 10 new astronauts out of more than 8,000 applicants in September 2025.
“For those who apply, becoming a Nasa astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at Nasa’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. “It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space.”
Since the 1960s, Nasa has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for increasingly challenging missions. The agency currently has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps.
Isaacman and other agency leaders recently laid out Nasa’s ambitions to return Americans to the moon in 2028. Both SpaceX and Blue Origin intend to support a crewed lunar landing.
All applicants must be US citizens, Nasa said, and have either a master’s degree in science, technology, engineering or mathematics; medical qualifications; training as a pilot; or two years’ work on a relevant doctoral program.
Three years of “related professional experience” are also required.
Applying pilots must have either 750 hours of pilot-in-command time of a high-performance jet, 1,500 total flight hours in another fixed-wing aircraft, or 1,000 total flight hours in a rotary-wing aircraft.
Applicants have until 11.59pm ET on Thursday, 3 December, to submit their applications.

items.desc: A tomb discovered in Siberia and associated with Scythians—a nomadic, horse-riding people that once roamed the Eurasian steppe—might provide the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use

Cannabis is one of the world’s most widely used psychoactive plants, with millions of people inhaling and ingesting it for its mind-­altering effects. But new research suggests our current relationship with weed is nothing new.
A study published November 5 in the journal Science suggests humans have been getting high on weed for at least 2,800 years—centuries longer than previously thought. The findings seem to offer the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use.
Researchers have long been interested in how ancient people used cannabis. Yet studying it has proven tricky because plants are rarely preserved over long periods of time. Since cannabis has many uses, including the production of oil and fiber, it’s even more challenging to determine whether and when individuals were using it specifically to get high.
In 2017, archaeologists digging in southern Siberia discovered a huge 2,800-year-old tomb that contained the remains of several high-status individuals . The site, called Tunnug 1, is associated with the Scythians , a nomadic, horse-riding culture that occupied the Eurasian steppe from the ninth to the third century B.C.E.
Excavations turned up numerous artifacts, from weapons and animal statues to pieces of gold jewelry and horse gear. But the researchers also found nearly 1,500 whole or partial cannabis seeds at the site, as well as preserved human hair, which allowed them to explore whether the Scythians might have been getting high.
“It’s only so often as an archaeologist that you get to drug test a person that’s been dead for nearly 3,000 years,” lead author Gino Caspari , an archaeologist at the University of Bern in Switzerland and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany, tells the New York Times ’ Annie Roth.
Radiocarbon dating traced the seeds to the early eighth century B.C.E., around the same time the burial site is believed to have been constructed. The hair, meanwhile, tested positive for pot. Specifically, the strands contained cannabinol (CBN), a byproduct of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive compound in the plant. It also contained weaker chemical signatures consistent with THC.
Caspari tells the Associated Press ’ Jamey Keaten and Philipp Jenne that it’s “extremely rare” for archaeologists to find “both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context.”

Doctors have made a potentially significant breakthrough in the hunt for a treatment for stiff person syndrome, the autoimmune condition that affects the singer Céline Dion .
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disease that attacks the central nervous system and can cause devastating rigidity throughout the body and painful muscle spasms. Despite decades of research, there is no cure.
Now a team of neurologists in the US trialling a novel form of immunotherapy have reported “exciting” and “very encouraging” results: the treatment has prompted dramatic improvements in people living with SPS.
Patients who previously needed help with basic daily tasks and struggled to walk have regained their ability to take part in everyday life, with some even returning to work and resuming hobbies, according to doctors at the Mayo Clinic.
The novel treatment, CAR-T cell therapy, is already used to treat cancer, and reprogrammes a patient’s immune cells to help fight disease. During the study, SPS patients’ own T cells, a type of immune cell, were extracted and engineered to wipe out disease-causing cells.
Neurologists said the results, published in medical journal Jama Neurology, were particularly exciting because patients had been able to return to activities they feared they would never be able to return to.
Dr Anastasia Zekeridou, a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, said: “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients.
“With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function. These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time.”
Jonathan Walden, one of the patients in the trial, had reached the point where walking and basic daily tasks required help from his family. But after CAR-T, he has returned to work.
“I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.”
Shari St Germain, another patient, had been suffering severe leg cramps and difficulty walking, and later even muscle rigidity and falls. But following CAR-T, she experienced major improvements. Every day feels “better and better”, she said.

809 years ago today, the Charter of the Forest was signed in England by King Henry III. This law document is sometimes described as the sister of the Magna Carta, and granted rights of free men to use the forests of England once reserved for King William I and his descendants. Many today learn from Robin Hood productions that the “kingswood” was a place where people couldn’t hunt or gather. The Charter of the Forest changed that and remained in force for centuries. HEAR what legal scholars have to say… (1217)
This charter was almost unique in providing a degree of economic protection for free men who used the forest to forage for food and to graze their animals. In contrast to Magna Carta, which dealt with the rights of barons, the Charter of the Forest restored to the common man some real rights, privileges, and protections against the abuses of an encroaching aristocracy.
Sir William Blackstone, the famous legal scholar and judge remarked in the eighteenth century that the “Charters of Liberties” which meant the Charter of the Forest and Magna Carta, were the most important accord of any kind to come out of the Middle Ages.

items.text:
A post shared by Pull Up A Sandbag (@spearhead_militaria)
While most people are putting their feet up in retirement, 103-year-old World War II veteran Irvin Koch is still keeping busy at his popular basement bar in Pasadena, Maryland. He’s been running his humble, fully licensed establishment for 60 years, where generations of customers regularly gather for a drink.
Koch served in the Philippines with the Navy, and when the war ended, he was 22 years old. Years later, in 1963, he and his brother bought a house in Pasadena that came with an unexpected bar in the basement. Rather than getting rid of it, he decided to open his very own dive bar called Sunset Knoll Club, now known as Irv’s Basement Bar. Six decades later, the drinks continue to flow, the regulars keep coming, the old jukebox keeps playing, and the original decor has barely changed.
Irv’s Basement Bar is full of quirky details, but the dozens of bras dangling from the ceiling are perhaps the most unexpected feature. Apparently, the collection has grown over the years as female customers have donated their own, often leaving their names behind as well. Irv can even recall who started the tradition—a customer named Amy. Visitors will also find names and messages scribbled across the bar counter, walls, and tables, left by other patrons who’ve visited the bar over the years.
Despite being tucked away in his home, the bar is officially recognized as a commercial establishment. And although Koch insists he stays open purely for the cash, his stepson, Jason Cook, believes there’s more to it. “He loves interacting with people and socializing,” he reveals . “He also likes being the center of attention. That certainly seems to be what’s keeping him alive.”

Since its advent, photography has changed the way we experience and remember culture. Portrait photography, in particular, helps to catalog those who have an outsized impact on society. A forthcoming exhibition at the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery looks back at portrait photography, what it can tell us about American history and culture, and how it helped shape the two. The show, titled Photographic Memory: Fifty Years of Collecting , features more than 120 works from the institution’s collection—including never-before-exhibited pieces.
Photographic Memory celebrates the 50th anniversary of the Portrait Gallery’s photographic repertoire. Photos now account for nearly half of the museum’s total holdings, but that wasn’t always the case. Photography didn’t enter the museum’s collection until 1976—the year of the U.S. bicentennial—when it expanded its collecting mandate to include photography. This shift mattered; without it, the Portrait Gallery couldn’t feature people important in U.S. history who never sat for a painted portrait or posed for a sculpture.
Although the show covers 50 years of collecting, some photographs in the exhibition are much older. One notable work includes a 1846 daguerreotype (the first publicly available photo process) of Dolley Madison by John Plumbe Jr. In the show, it’s paired with a 1843 half-plate daguerreotype of President John Quincy Adams. This marks the first time that the earliest known photograph of a U.S. president and a first lady have been shown together.
Other pieces in Photographic Memory include iconic images and people beyond politicians. These works include Alexander Gardner’s original “cracked plate” portrait of Abraham Lincoln, images of athletes like Muhammad Ali, singers including Billie Holiday, and artists such as Georgia O’Keeffe and Isamu Noguchi . The exhibition also debuts a portrait of poet and author Amanda Gorman, photographed by Shawn Theodore, and a portrait of actor and activist Christopher Reeve by Herb Ritts. The exhibition also features influential photographers, including Alfred Stieglitz, Dorothea Lange , Ansel Adams , and Gordon Parks .

items.text:
It’s a time-honoured treatment and rubbing certainly helps, but other leaves could be just as good
I f you’ve ever brushed against a stinging nettle, chances are someone told you to find a dock leaf. The wide green leaves of dock plants seem to grow conveniently nearby, and rubbing one on a sting is a time-honoured remedy. But does it actually work?
Probably not in any way that’s unique to the plant, says John Tregoning, a professor at Imperial College London and the author of Live Forever? A Curious Scientist’s Guide to Wellness, Ageing and Death .
When you brush against a nettle, tiny hairs on the plant can pierce the skin and release a mixture of chemicals, including histamine, acetylcholine and serotonin. These trigger burning, itching and redness.
Could dock leaves contain chemicals that counteract the sting, such as antihistamines? “Maybe, but probably not,” says Tregoning. There is little evidence that dock leaf sap contains substances capable of significantly relieving the reaction.
So why do people swear by them? Rubbing a leaf against the skin may provide a competing sensation that temporarily distracts from the pain, says Tregoning. “There’s a limit to the number of sensations that the nerve cells can process, so if you overstimulate them with the rubbing there’s less feedback from the pain.”
The distraction of searching for the leaves may also help. “The short burst of pain is relieved in the time spent hunting for the dock leaves.” Tregoning suggests that applying the sap may also have a cooling or soothing effect. But none of these things are unique to dock leaves.
A small study compared dock leaves with lettuce leaves as a treatment for nettle stings in nine medical students. It found no meaningful difference between the two. Tregoning suspects that any perceived benefit is most likely to be a placebo effect.

items.title: Stolen During the Nazi Occupation of Orléans, France, This Painting Was Rediscovered After 86 Years With Help From Wild West-Inspired 'Wanted' Posters
items.desc: The Musée des Beaux-Arts d'Orléans is on a mission to retrieve hundreds of missing artworks from its collections. It recently tracked down a 17th-century painting by Dutch artist Willem Cornelisz Duyster right before it went to auction in Switzerland
items.text:
In June 1940, amid the chaos of the Nazi siege of Orléans , France, someone stole a 17th-century painting from a local museum. Now, with the help of a creative campaign, the looted painting has been located and is on its way back to the museum for the first time in 86 years.
The piece in question is Un Buveur (The Drinker) . Painted by Dutch artist Willem Cornelisz Duyster around the year 1630, it depicts a man seated in a chair, an empty glass in one hand and his other hand raised as if making a point in conversation.
It was housed at the Musée Paul Fourché, an annex of the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans , when Germans invaded the city early in World War II. It’s not clear who stole the piece, as both German troops and French locals are suspected of plundering the museum’s unguarded collection.
Until a few weeks ago, the painting’s whereabouts were unknown for decades. In July, the museum launched a campaign intended to raise awareness about the 424 stolen, looted and displaced artworks that are still missing from its collection. As part of the initiative, the museum created a series of black-and-white, Wild West-inspired posters featuring various missing works with the word “WANTED” splashed across in bold yellow type.
The campaign is based on a digital catalog of the works the museum created and distributed to galleries, auction houses, law firms and other art-market professionals.
“If a presumed stolen work were to resurface at a public sale or in an estate, we’ll be able to flag it,” Olivia Voisin , the museum’s director, told Le Monde ’s Victor Riallais in July. “Times have changed; professionals are wary of the risk of handling stolen goods. We're providing solid evidence, precise clues, so that no one can ever again tell us, ‘We didn’t know.’”
The eye-catching posters were shared on the museum’s social media pages, website and beyond. They caught the eye of an unnamed Orléans resident, who took it upon himself to help search for the looted works. He was clicking through online auction listings one day when he spotted a piece that was described as a study of Un Buveur . Estimated to be worth about $3,400, it was due to be sold by the Gloggner auction house in Lucerne, Switzerland, on October 17.
The man alerted museum officials, who determined that the piece was the original—not a study. When they presented their evidence, the painting’s current owner “immediately proposed to restitute the painting” at no cost, Voisin tells ARTnews ’ Devorah Lauter.

A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.
As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.
America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

A natural gas utility in Vermont struck a first-in-the-nation deal that will soon be saving customers money by turning to geothermal energy.
Vermont Gas launched the state’s “first community-scale geothermal project,” something the company’s CEO called one of the best solutions for lowering energy costs and one that many homeowners across the country hope to see in other areas.
These systems can indeed provide serious savings. A case study published by the DoE on an apartment complex in New York found that its geothermal heat pumps helped reduce energy costs by 40.7% across the 72-unit site.
Opened back in 2016, residents have seen average annual cost savings of approximately $24,000 per year, by now reaching a staggering quarter-million dollars in savings.
To that end, Vermont Gas has partnered with geothermal developer Dandelion Energy to install super efficient geothermal heating and cooling to the 44-unit Riggs Meadow affordable housing development in Hinesburg.
Drilling down into heated pockets of water below the Earth will begin in early 2027, while residents will be able to move in by year’s end.
The more high-profile geothermal installations in the US typically power large infrastructure, like Fervo Energy’s Corsac Station that ultimately serves Google-owned data centers. Yet others see the technology as ideal for utilities in modest-income housing.
In Detroit’s Virginia Park, the 27-unit Merrill Place II housing development for low and middle-income earners was designed with a geothermal heating and cooling system that, according to a release from the Mayor’s office , will make these utilities “free.”
“Our tenants are not billed separately for heating and cooling, which removes one of the most unpredictable and burdensome household expenses,” explained Sauda Ahmad-Green, lead developer on the project.
“That stability matters. It allows families to plan, to breathe a little easier, and to focus on building their futures instead of worrying about utility spikes.”

items.title: What is the Paris Agreement and why does 1.5C matter?
items.desc: The 2015 pact is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.
items.text:
Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from a fund for damages linked to climate change after flash floods in August 2026
In Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement designed to limit global warming to 1.5C and avoid its worst impacts.
But despite some progress in areas like renewable energy, the world has continued to warm at a rapid pace.
A recent UN report said the target was likely to be breached in the next few years and that "urgent and stringent" action would be needed to return the world to 1.5C.
The Paris Agreement is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.
It came into force on 4 November 2016 and saw almost all the nations of the world agree to cut the greenhouse gas emissions which cause global warming.
However, the United States - the world's second biggest greenhouse gas emitter - withdrew from the deal in January 2026 under President Donald Trump.
The US also withdrew during Trump's first presidency, but it rejoined in 2021 under his successor President Joe Biden.
The only other UN member states outside the Paris agreement are Iran, Libya and Yemen.
The Paris Agreement lists a series of commitments:
to "pursue efforts" to limit global temperature rises to 1.5C, and to keep them "well below" 2.0C above those recorded in pre-industrial times, generally considered to mean the late 19th Century
to achieve a balance - known as net zero - between the greenhouse gases that humans put into the atmosphere and the gases that they actively remove, in the second half of this century
each country to set its own emission-reduction targets, reviewed every five years to raise ambitions
richer countries to help poorer nations by providing funding, known as climate finance, to adapt to climate change and switch to renewable energy
The 1.5C target is generally accepted to refer to a 20-year average rather than a single year.
So, while 2024 was more than 1.5C warmer than pre-industrial times , it did not mean the Paris Agreement threshold has been breached
Every 0.1C of warming brings with it greater risks for the planet, such as longer heatwaves, more intense storms and wildfires, according to climate scientists .
But a very large body of scientific evidence shows that warming of 2C or more would bring far greater impacts, on top of those felt at 1.5C, UN scientists say.

items.text:
I just want to be in a place like this by Steen Foege
Landscape painting has appealed to artists since ancient times, and contemporary creatives continue to capture nature’s beauty with paint. At Nightingale Gallery in Melbourne, Australia, a group exhibition titled A Certain Slant of Light brought together seven artists who celebrate nature in their own distinct styles.
The show featured paintings by Angeline Bartholomeusz , Sharman Feinberg , Steen Foege , Suzanne Ganjineh , Jon Hewitt , Wendy Jagger , and Jessica Olpp . All seven artists draw inspiration from the natural landscapes around them, but each offers a unique perspective, capturing nature’s light, color, texture, and atmosphere in different ways.
Oil painter Jessica Olpp is known for her serene, often muted depictions of clouds drifting over open fields. She began painting as a meditative counterbalance to her career as a French teacher, and describes her work as reflecting “a quiet lyricism and deep appreciation for stillness.” Jon Hewitt and Steen Foege are also inspired by clouds. They bring stunning color to their sky paintings, using soft pastels and bold, vivid hues. Their work captures the magic of a changing sky, especially when clouds light up in shades of pink at sunrise and sunset.
Meanwhile, Sharman Feinberg’s colorful work captures the everyday life in her neighborhood, where parkland and rows of houses sit side by side. Wendy Jagger creates expressive, textured depictions of coastlines, and Angeline Bartholomeusz creates stunning tree paintings inspired by multiple horizons. Last but not least, Suzanne Ganjineh uses watercolor to paint her stunning scenes on linen.

items.title: The Arctic Polar Vortex Is Collapsing Earlier in the Season Than Ever Documented—but We Don't Know How It'll Affect Global Weather
items.desc: A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the Great Texas Freeze in 2021. This time, the ongoing "super" El Niño might offset some of the collapse's influence
items.text:
Something strange is happening in the skies above the Arctic: the polar vortex is collapsing unusually early.
The polar vortex is a ring of westerly winds that forms about 10 to 30 miles above the Earth’s surface, which generally keeps the coldest air sequestered around the North Pole. It usually reaches its peak intensity in December and January and weakens later in the season.
This year, however, it’s already showing signs of disruption. Forecasts suggest that the polar vortex could collapse within the next week, report Joe Wertz and Mary Hui at Bloomberg . This extraordinary occurrence, combined with the “super” El Niño, could influence global weather patterns in ways that scientists are still trying to understand.
“As a weather fan, this is a big event because it’s so unprecedented,” says Judah Cohen , a climatologist at MIT, to Jackie Flynn Mogensen at Scientific American . “It’s a lot of excitement. Everybody’s hair is on fire in the climate or meteorologist community.”
When the polar vortex weakens, it can lead to something called sudden stratospheric warming (SSW). This phenomenon occurs when temperatures in the stratosphere , a layer of the Earth’s atmosphere, dramatically spike within just a few days. The temperature increase can weaken or even reverse the west-to-east winds of the polar vortex, sometimes causing the vortex to split apart. As a result, the cold air that is usually trapped within the stratosphere can be pushed south.
We reside in an atmospheric layer called the troposphere. The stratosphere sits above it, stretching from about 6.2 miles to 31 miles above Earth’s surface, and it contains the ozone layer .
Researchers have been keeping reliable records of these events since 1958, and only two other SSWs have been documented in November, says Laura Ciasto , a meteorologist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, to Doyle Rice and Dinah Voyles Pulver at USA Today . Previously, the earliest polar vortex disruption happened on November 28 in 1968, reports Scientific American.
These events can have wide-ranging impacts. In 2021, a disruption pushed cold air into Texas , leading to the Great Texas Freeze . The devastating chill caused more than 200 deaths and left more than 4.5 million homes and businesses without power because of the enormous strain on the state’s power grid.
That doesn’t mean the same thing will happen this winter. For now, researchers are unsure how the collapsing polar vortex’s influence will interact

items.title: Where Did Stonehenge's Mysterious, Six-Ton Altar Stone Really Come From? Geologists Rule Out the Scottish Hypothesis as the Search Deepens
items.desc: A comprehensive investigation of the sandstone megalith’s "geological fingerprint" suggests it did not originate in northeast Scotland, as a surprising study concluded in 2024, sending scientists back into the field to track down the enigmatic slab's origins
items.text:
At the heart of Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain lies a flat, six-ton slab of sandstone whose origin has long baffled scientists. This mystery was seemingly solved in 2024 when the stone was linked to a potential source in northeast Scotland, at least 465 miles away by land. Now, a rigorous follow-up investigation has overturned that shocking conclusion, revealing that researchers were likely hunting across the wrong terrain.
A new study published this week in the Journal of the Geological Society compared the Altar Stone’s detailed geological signature with field samples gathered across the alleged origin site in Scotland’s Orcadian Basin . The findings determined that the slab’s true origin remains an unresolved puzzle, marking the latest chapter in an evolving scientific detective story about where distinctive 16-foot slab originated.

Scientists from Leipzig evaluated whether volunteer handlers and their dogs could be trained as effective detectives, and found the teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy.
Other methods to combat invasive species have been costly and time-consuming, and the lack of effective early-detection methods has limited ecologists’ ability to control further colonization by invasive species.
Dr. Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth and her colleagues at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) tested the feasibility of a volunteer dog-handler training program, so citizen scientists could join the fight.

items.text:
Bats primarily use echolocation to hunt prey, using their sophisticated biological sonar systems to find and capture tasty insects in the dark. But some moths have evolved a clever workaround to these attacks: They use their genitalia to produce high-frequency sound waves that essentially scramble their pursuers’ sonar, causing them to miss their intended target and fly away hungry.
This is such an effective strategy for staving off bat attacks that it’s arisen in moths independently up to seven times between 5 million and 30 million years ago, researchers report in a study published November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B .
Different lineages of hawkmoths —a group of large, agile pollinators—have separately evolved similar solutions to the same problem, a phenomenon known as convergent evolution . The findings highlight how “interactions between predators and their prey can drive the evolution of complex and sometimes bizarre adaptations,” lead author ​​Paul Masonick , an evolutionary biologist at the Florida Museum of Natural History, tells IFLScience ’s Rachael Funnell.
“Bat predation has been a major driver of insect evolution,” he adds. “It has contributed significantly to the remarkable diversity of bioacoustic defenses among moths that we see today.”
Hawkmoths, also known as sphinx moths, are sturdy, nocturnal insects known for hovering in mid-air while sipping nectar from flowers, just like hummingbirds. Scientists estimate there are 1,600 species of hawkmoths around the world, with most occupying warm, wet tropical regions.
Many species of hawkmoths use ultrasound to fend off bats, often by scraping their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, producing noise via stridulation . Scientists don’t know why moths first evolved these ultrasound-producing systems, but they suspect the behavior initially arose to help males attract mates.
“In all the species that make the noise, the males have to go to a lot of effort to impress a female,” Ian Kitching , an entomologist at the Natural History Museum in London who provided images of moths for the study, says in a statement . “This may have been the original use for the sounds. GNN Voices is a new series of first-person pieces from people worth listening to: practitioners, researchers, teachers, and neighbors sharing what they’ve learned and how they see things.
My dad’s name was Kiran. In Sanskrit, it means “a ray of light.”
I wrote my book, Making Sense of Purpose , in his memory. His name is in the subtitle.
My dad found a way to walk with people without carrying them; he found a way to guide them without giving them directions; he held space, he held hands, he held space for their wants, needs and expectations, and then he shined a light on what made them and mattered to them and what’s forward …
This week is Diwali, the festival of lights. This year, I want to make it a gift to everyone. A week to shine a light back on the year and move forward with purpose before we rush into the new one.
Wanting to avoid a doom scroll is hard. But giving people something to do instead maybe helps.
It happens more because of the environment we built than because of any flaw in us. We grab what fills us without considering whether it nourishes us.
A few minutes of reflection pays us back. Researchers at Harvard Business School found that new employees who spent the last 15 minutes of each training day writing and reflecting on what they’d learned performed 22.8% better on their final test.
Ten questions. Five days. One in the morning, one at night. A few minutes each. Write it down, or just reflect and take note. Either way counts.
We’re bad at knowing what will make us happy. We rarely get explicit about what made a good moment good. So we never ask people what made them happy; we ask what makes them smile as they reflect.
We are strengths to be harnessed. Not weaknesses to be fixed. And our values are who we are when the world is at its messiest. Kennon Sheldon and Andrew Elliot found that when our goals come from our values, we put in more sustained effort and are more likely to reach them.
Not every plateau needs to be broken. Self-forgiveness is the single most powerful action, wholly within your control, that allows you to empty your backpack. When we forgive ourselves, the likelihood going forward is that we’ll be faster to break free than if we carry the guilt forward. And big wins are made by small steps.
As David McRaney puts it, Anxiety = Fear + Uncertainty. Sorting what we can control, what we can influence and what is outside our control makes uncertainty feel less overwhelming. And compassion is about caring, not carrying.

The animal has disappeared from much of the countryside with conservationists warning of a long-term collapse in its population.
However, new data suggests dormouse numbers increased between 2020-2025, a period that coincided with warmer springs and summers.
Scientists believe these conditions may help dormice survive, by boosting food supplies and reducing the time they spend asleep.

The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the conservation charity People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES), has been monitoring sites in England and Wales since 1998.
It found that since 2000, dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60%, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5%.

Great Square of Pegasus’s four corners are widely visible, but its inner stars provide a useful indicator of darkness
This week, we are going to locate the Great Square of Pegasus and count stars to see how dark your sky is.
The chart shows the view looking south from London at 2000 GMT on 9 November. High in the sky is the Great Square of Pegasus, a distinctive pattern of four stars that marks the body of the mythical winged horse.
The four corner stars – Alpheratz, Scheat, Markab and Algenib – are bright enough to be visible even from suburban locations. The question is, how many stars can you see inside the square?
To do the experiment, find somewhere away from direct lighting and wait for at least 20 minutes to allow your eyes time to adjust to the darkness. No checking your phone to pass the time, as the bright screen will ruin your dark adaptation. Then look carefully inside the square and count every star that you can see with your naked eyes. Do not include the four corner stars.
If you can see just one star, your sky is relatively poor . Four stars indicate an average sky, while seven suggests good conditions. Count 13 and your sky is very good indeed. If you can see about 35, you are observing under an exceptionally dark sky.

Benefits of baxdrostat are unexpectedly found to remain up to two years after patients stop taking it
Millions of people with high blood pressure stand to benefit from a new drug that has stunned doctors by reversing a common cause of the condition for years after patients stopped taking the medication.
Patients who took the drug, called baxdrostat, saw their blood pressure improve during a six- to 12-month course of the daily pills, but unexpectedly the benefits remained up to two years later, with some patients no longer on any hypertension drugs and potentially cured of the condition.
“It’s very exciting to see,” said Prof Morris Brown, a hypertension specialist at Queen Mary University of London, who led the study. “Just under a quarter of the patients came off all treatment and had completely normal blood pressure.”
More than a billion people worldwide have high blood pressure, or hypertension, including more than 12 million in the UK. In 5 to 10% of cases, the condition is caused by small nodules or benign tumours on the adrenal glands that cause them to overproduce a hormone called aldosterone. The excess hormone raises blood pressure by signalling the kidneys to retain salt.
The standard treatment for what is called primary aldosteronism is to surgically remove the affected adrenal gland, but other factors can contribute to the patient’s hypertension, meaning surgery is not always a complete cure.
Baxdrostat is known as an aldosterone synthase inhibitor (ASI) which suppresses the blood pressure-raising hormone. The drug was approved in the US earlier this year for patients with hypertension that is not controlled by existing drugs. It is being assessed by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice), which could make the drug available through the NHS next year.
The potentially curative effect of baxdrostat came to light in a small study that followed 14 patients whose hypertension improved dramatically during a three-month trial of the drug. They continued taking the daily pills for six to 12 months and then stopped. When doctors checked the patients up to two years later, their blood pressure was still lower. Details are published in the New England Journal of Medicine .

“For projects with minimally effective communication, only 37% finish on time, 48% are completed within budget, and 52% meet their set goal," an excerpt from their findings read.
The experts were a panel of engineers and construction consultants who have since advocated for “establishing robust communication channels” to ensure everyone is aligned and informed about potential issues.
The bigger question here is how much these botched construction jobs cost. According to recent industry insights , the price tag can reach $177 billion annually.
The same findings point to a common cause behind 48% of all rework: poor communication and bad project data.
Further insights reveal that 22% of the work comes from “bad or inaccessible project information.” But how do these communication breakdowns happen? Over the phone, apparently.
According to the data, only 10% of phone-based decisions typically get formally documented. That means 90% of those critical conversations can't be revisited when needed.

61 years ago today, the ironically-named Murder Act of 1965 is given Royal Assent, formally abolishing the death penalty in the United Kingdom for almost all crimes. Introduced by MP for Liverpool Sydney Silverman, it replaced hanging with mandatory sentences of life-imprisonment in all but 4 cases. The outstanding exceptions related to military-intelligence crimes, such as piracy with the intent to cause grievous injury, high treason, and espionage. READ more… (1965)
No executions have occurred in the United Kingdom since the Murder Act of 1965. The last were on August 13th, 1964, when Peter Allen and Gwynne Evans were hanged for murdering John Alan West during a theft four months earlier.
During the Troubles Westminster passed the Northern Ireland Constitution Act 1973, abolishing Stormont, and the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1973, abolishing the death penalty for murder there. The death penalty was not fully abolished in the United Kingdom until 1998 by the Human Rights Act 1998 and the Crime and Disorder Act 1998.
735 years ago today, the Republic of Venice passed a law confining the city’s growing glassmaking industry to the island of Murano , giving birth to the tradition of Murano glass, one of the city’s most iconic characteristics. In the following century, exports began, and the island became famous, initially for glass beads and mirrors. Aventurine glass was invented on the island, and for a while Murano was the main producer of glass in Europe. Today, it’s a craft that is entering the fine art world.
From practical items like cups, bowls, lamps, and chandeliers, Murano artisans gradually began turning from applied art to fine art, with chandeliers becoming works of sculpture, and works of sculpture becoming masterpieces.
While the glass itself is delicate and dainty, a Murano glass artisan must be physically durable and resilient. Once he or she starts a piece, they cannot stop until it’s finished even if that means 16 hours of work. Neither the artisan, nor the glass can be allowed to cool down too much from the incredible heat of the furnaces, otherwise, the molten glass won’t be shapable anymore.
Murano glass artwork is now a more sensible business model for these artisans, as the high cost they merit is more flexible and can absorb higher energy prices in Europe as natural gas is needed to heat the furnaces.

items.title: Strange Gas in Mars' Atmosphere Hints the Red Planet Is Still Volcanically Active—and Points to Places to Search for Alien Life
items.desc: Cracks along a giant Martian volcano, possibly above a magma chamber, might be spewing magmatic gases into the atmosphere, according to a new study. The fissures might host environments akin to Earth's hydrothermal vents, where life on our planet may have emerged
items.text:
Volcanic activity shaped the Red Planet for hundreds of millions of years . But today, researchers aren’t sure whether our neighbor has retained some of that volcanic feistiness or if it is truly dead inside.
In a study published November 4 in the journal Science Advances , scientists suggest that magma is, indeed, still on the move beneath the surface of Mars. Their evidence comes from unexpected gas detection in the planet’s atmosphere, which may have been spewed from fresh cracks on its Alba Mons volcano. If confirmed, their findings could shape how researchers search for signs of extraterrestrial life on Mars.
It’s not the first time researchers have found possible hints of ongoing volcanic activity on the Red Planet. NASA’s InSight lander has previously detected marsquakes whose rumblings indicated potentially active subsurface fluid .
“Some folks think it’s magma; others think it’s water,” Tracy Gregg , a planetary volcanologist at the University at Buffalo, who didn’t participate in the study, tells National Geographic ’s Robin George Andrews. “I think it might be both.”
Mars’ shield volcano Olympus Mons is the tallest mountain in the solar system. It’s around 4.5 times the height of Mount Everest.
The new work provides the strongest evidence yet discovered of gases released by dormant Martian volcanoes, complementing Insight’s data, lead author Alexander Trokhimovskiy , a planetary scientist at the Space Research Institute at the Russian Academy of Sciences, tells Live Science ’s Elizabeth Howell.
The gas in question is hydrogen chloride , a stinky substance that can come from volcanoes on Earth. In 2021, the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO), a collaboration between the European Space Agency and Russia’s Roscosmos, recorded unexpected spikes of the smelly gas above Mars’ northern hemisphere during its early summer. Usually, atmospheric hydrogen chloride peaks in the northern hemisphere’s winter and then almost disappears over the summer.
The researchers found that the gassy deviation happened during multiple Mars years, each of which is nearly as long as two Earth years . What’s more, it always occurred in the early summer and over volcanic fissures on the edges of Alba Mons , a giant shield volcano spanning roughly the area of the contiguous United States.
Images snapped by TGO’s high-resolution camera revealed new, narrow cracks. The photos also showed color changes on Mars’ surface, which the researchers suspect are related.

items.title: One of the year's most prolific meteor showers visible in the night sky throughout November
items.desc: The Leonid meteor shower, known for its bright and fast meteors continues through November.
items.text:
The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.
The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.
There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.
The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.
These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.
Experts advise finding a safe, dark location away from sources of light pollution such as street lights.
The meteors will be visible with the naked eye, with no binoculars or telescope required.
However, giving your eyes some time to adapt to the dark - perhaps 20 or 30 minutes - will give you the best chance of spotting them.
A wide open space is the best place to be, giving a full view of the night sky.
Meteors could be visible anywhere but the Leonids' radiant - the point from which they seem to appear - will, as the name suggests, be around the head of the constellation Leo, meaning this is the best part of the sky to focus your gaze.
As with all celestial spectacles, clear skies will be a must.
Viewing conditions could be particularly good around the meteor shower peak in the middle of November.
This is because the Moon will be below the horizon around midnight, meaning its reflected light will be less likely to spoil the view.

items.desc: Rising global temperatures mean extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense.
items.text:
In January 2026, wildfires in Chile caused the evacuation of more than 50,000 people
Many extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense around the world, fuelled by human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels.
Here are four ways that rising temperatures are affecting weather extremes.
Even a small increase in average temperatures makes a big difference to heat extremes.
As the range of daily temperatures shifts to warmer levels, hotter days become more likely and more intense.
Scientists use computer models to simulate how individual extreme weather events unfold in two scenarios:
today's world with about 1.4C , external of human-caused warming
a hypothetical world without human influence on the climate
That way, they can estimate , external how much a particular heatwave, storm or drought was affected by climate change.
The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Five widespread heatwaves affected the country, resulting in 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).
Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy, described summer 2026 as "remarkable" and warned that extreme heat events would only become more common as the world warms.

Climate change has also intensified multiple heatwaves across the world this year, according to scientists at the World Weather Attribution group (WWA).
Examples include Australia's worst heatwave in six years in January, the 45C that India experienced in April and Europe's deadly June temperatures .
Heatwaves can happen as a result of heat domes , external , which are created when an area of high pressure stays over the same area for days or weeks, trapping hot air underneath.
Higher temperatures in the Arctic - which has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average , external - may be affecting the fast band of winds high in the atmosphere known as the jet stream.
One theory suggests that this is making heat domes more likely, although this is not clear cut.
For every 1C rise in air temperature, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more moisture , external .
With more moisture available, rainfall can become heavier.

items.title: A really simple guide to climate change
items.desc: Human activities are causing the world to heat up, posing serious threats to people and nature.
items.text:
Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events
Human activities are causing world temperatures to rise, posing serious threats to people and nature.
Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.
Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.
Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.
2024 was Earth's hottest year on record , with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.
It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service , external .
Temperatures remained high in 2025 , despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.
The opposite El Niño pattern , combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.
The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.
But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).
This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.
When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.
Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50% .
The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels , external has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.
Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:
more frequent and intense extreme weather , such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall
rapid melting of glaciers and ice sheets, contributing to sea-level rises
warmer oceans , which can fuel more intense storms and harm sea life
These changes are already having serious consequences for people and economies around the world.
